a plus b, in brackets, squared, equals a squared plus b squared. Almost everyone writes this on a test. And it's wrong!
Today you'll see with one simple picture what the answer really is. And you'll learn all three binomial formulas, plus a few mental math tricks that will impress everyone.
Chapter one: What does squared actually mean?
Squared means: multiply something by itself. So a plus b squared is a plus b times a plus b.
Let's test it with numbers. Three plus four is seven. Seven squared is forty-nine.
But three squared plus four squared is nine plus sixteen, which is only twenty-five. Twenty-four are missing! We forgot something.
This is why so many students lose points on tests. But luckily, there's a picture that makes sure you never forget it again.
Chapter two: The picture that explains everything.
We draw a square with side length a plus b. Its area is exactly a plus b squared.
Now we split each side into a and b. In the top left we get a square a times a, so a squared. In the bottom right a square b times b, so b squared.
But there are two more rectangles! Each one is a times b. These are exactly what most people forget.
Together that gives: a squared plus two a b plus b squared. That's the first binomial formula.
With our numbers: nine plus sixteen plus two times twelve. That's the missing twenty-four! Together forty-nine. It works!
Remember the picture: one big square, one small square, and two equal rectangles. If you can see that, you'll never write the formula wrong again.
Chapter three: Expanding the brackets.
You can also get the formula without the picture. Every term in the first bracket gets multiplied by every term in the second bracket.
a times a is a squared. a times b is a b. b times a is another a b. And b times b is b squared. Two a b, just like in the picture.
An example: x plus three squared. That's x squared plus two times three x plus nine. So x squared plus six x plus nine.
One more: two x plus one squared. Front: two x squared, so four x squared. Middle: two times two x times one, so four x. At the end: one. Result: four x squared plus four x plus one.
Chapter four: The second binomial formula.
Now with a minus: a minus b squared. That gives a squared minus two a b plus b squared.
Careful: only the middle term gets a minus. The b squared at the end always stays plus, because minus b times minus b is plus.
Example: x minus five squared. That's x squared minus ten x plus twenty-five.
Let's check with numbers: ten minus one squared is nine squared, which is eighty-one. And with the formula: one hundred minus twenty plus one. Also eighty-one!

Chapter five: The third binomial formula.
a plus b times a minus b. Something beautiful happens here: the result is simply a squared minus b squared.
Why? When you expand, you get plus a b once and minus a b once. They cancel out exactly. Only a squared and minus b squared are left.
Example: x plus seven times x minus seven. That's simply x squared minus forty-nine. No middle term!
Chapter six: Mental math like a pro.
What is ninety-nine squared? Write it as one hundred minus one, squared. That's ten thousand minus two hundred plus one. So nine thousand eight hundred and one.
Or twenty-one squared: twenty plus one, squared. Four hundred plus forty plus one equals four hundred and forty-one.
And forty-nine times fifty-one? That's fifty minus one times fifty plus one. Third formula: two thousand five hundred minus one, so two thousand four hundred and ninety-nine. In two seconds!
Chapter seven: Using the formulas backwards.
Often you have to recognize the formula the other way around. x squared plus eight x plus sixteen. Here sixteen is four squared, and eight x is two times four x. So this is x plus four squared.
And x squared minus thirty-six? That's a squared minus b squared. So x plus six times x minus six.
Pro tip: you'll need exactly this backwards trick later for completing the square and for solving quadratic equations.
Chapter eight: The three most common mistakes.
Mistake number one: a plus b squared equals a squared plus b squared. The middle term two a b is missing.
Mistake number two: x minus three squared equals x squared minus nine. The correct answer is x squared minus six x plus nine.
Mistake number three: forgetting the two in the middle. x plus five squared has ten x in the middle, not five x.
